messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 61

James is twenty-one years old, a chef at a busy farm-to-table restaurant in the city, and he has not been able to sleep through the night in eleven months. He shows up for his afternoon shift at four, but lately he has been coming in at two, just to sit in the walk-in cooler with the door cracked, letting the cold air wash over his arms. He tells me the cold helps him think. He tells me he cannot think at all.

The story he tells begins a year ago, when he was still a line cook at a different place, a fast-casual spot that did not care about its staff. He was twenty, fresh from culinary school, working doubles to prove himself. There was a sous chef there, a man ten years older, who took James under his wing. James admired him. The man taught him how to break down a chicken, how to season by feel, how to move through a rush without panic. James trusted him.

One night, after close, the sous chef asked James to stay and help with inventory. The rest of the crew had gone. The lights in the dining room were off. James remembers the hum of the walk-in freezer, the smell of bleach and old grease. He remembers the sous chef’s hand on his shoulder, then his neck, then the small of his back. He remembers freezing. He remembers thinking, *This is not what I think it is.* He remembers not saying no. He remembers not saying anything.

What happened next, James describes in fragments. The concrete floor against his cheek. The sous chef’s weight. The sound of his own breathing, too fast, like he was running. Afterward, the sous chef helped him stand up, handed him a towel, and said, “You’re okay. You’re fine. Let’s not make this weird.” James drove home in silence. He showered for forty minutes. He did not tell anyone.

The next day, he went back to work. He stayed for three more months. He says he does not know why. He says he kept thinking if he just acted normal, it would stop feeling real. But it did not stop. Every time the sous chef walked past him, James’s stomach dropped. Every time a hand touched his shoulder—a coworker reaching for a plate, a customer tapping him for ketchup—he flinched. He started dropping things. His knife work got sloppy. He cut himself twice in one week, on purpose, he thinks, though he is not sure.

He left that job without giving notice. He found the new place, the farm-to-table restaurant, and told himself it was a fresh start. But the symptoms followed him. He cannot stand being in the walk-in freezer for more than a few seconds—the hum, the cold, the door clicking shut—so he uses the cooler instead, even though it is less efficient. He avoids the back hallway where the dry goods are stored because it reminds him of the inventory room. He cannot have anyone stand behind him while he works the grill. He has snapped at two dishwashers for approaching him from behind. He knows it is irrational. He feels ashamed.

At night, he does not sleep. He lies awake replaying the details, or he dreams about them and wakes up with his heart pounding, convinced the sous chef is in his apartment. He has started drinking after his shift, just enough to dull the edge, but it does not help. He has stopped seeing friends. He has not been on a date since it happened. He tells me he feels like he is living behind glass, watching himself go through the motions of being a chef, being a son, being a person, but none of it feels real.

He is here because his mother called him last week and said he sounded hollow. He did not know what else to do.
